claim: Neuroeconomics proposes that a major step in decision-making is the compression of relevant features defining different goods into a single dimension of value.
source: Neuroeconomics holds that a major step in this process is the compression of the relevant features defining the different goods into a single dimension of value, so that disparate goods can be compared on a universal scale (Levy and Glimcher, 2012; Padoa-Schioppa, 2011; Padoa-Schioppa et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature in the field of neuroeconomics.

claim: Neural activity in the orbitofrontal cortex tracks value on a universal scale during economic choice.
source: Single-unit and fMRI studies have typically assigned this process to the orbitofrontal cortex (OFC) based on the demonstration that neural activity there – identified either by single-unit or BOLD response – tracks value on this universal scale during economic choice (Levy and Glimcher, 2011; McGinty et al., 2016; Padoa-Schioppa, 2009; Padoa-Schioppa and Assad, 2006; Padoa-Schioppa and Assad, 2008; Plassmann et al., 2010; Plassmann et al., 2007; Rich and Wallis, 2016; Tremblay and Schultz, 1999; Xie and Padoa-Schioppa, 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to single-unit and fMRI studies.

claim: Single-units in orbitofrontal cortex often do not encode value independent of other information.
source: Yet these correlates are not ubiquitous; often single-units in orbitofrontal cortex do not seem to encode value independent of other information (Blanchard et al., 2015; Kennerley et al., 2011; Kennerley and Wallis, 2009; McDannald et al., 2014; Wikenheiser et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to studies showing inconsistent value encoding in OFC.

claim: Causal evidence to support a critical role for the OFC in economic choice is sparse.
source: Further, causal evidence to support a critical role for the OFC in economic choice is sparse, owing to the difficulty in doing such experiments in humans or monkeys, where economic choice is typically studied.
evidence: This claim is based on the authors' assessment of the literature and the practical challenges of conducting causal experiments.

claim: Rats' behavior in the economic choice task exhibited all the core features of economic choice.
source: Although rats' behavior in this task exhibited all the core features of economic choice (Levy and Glimcher, 2012; Padoa-Schioppa, 2011; Padoa-Schioppa et al., 2006), it was entirely insensitive to optogenetic inactivation of the lateral OFC, inactivation which was sufficient to disrupt devaluation-sensitive changes in Pavlovian responding (Gardner, 2017.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to literature defining core features of economic choice and by reference to prior work by the authors.

claim: Optogenetic inactivation of lateral OFC did not affect economic choice behavior in rats.
source: Although rats' behavior in this task exhibited all the core features of economic choice (Levy and Glimcher, 2012; Padoa-Schioppa, 2011; Padoa-Schioppa et al., 2006), it was entirely insensitive to optogenetic inactivation of the lateral OFC, inactivation which was sufficient to disrupt devaluation-sensitive changes in Pavlovian responding (Gardner, 2017.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to the authors' prior published work.

claim: Lateral OFC inactivation was sufficient to disrupt devaluation-sensitive changes in Pavlovian responding.
source: Although rats' behavior in this task exhibited all the core features of economic choice (Levy and Glimcher, 2012; Padoa-Schioppa, 2011; Padoa-Schioppa et al., 2006), it was entirely insensitive to optogenetic inactivation of the lateral OFC, inactivation which was sufficient to disrupt devaluation-sensitive changes in Pavlovian responding (Gardner, 2017.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to the authors' prior published work.

claim: Lateral OFC is not generally necessary for established choice behavior.
source: Indeed recent work suggests that lateral OFC is not generally necessary for established choice behavior (Miller et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to recent published work.

claim: The OFC consists of several subregions.
source: The OFC is increasingly recognized as consisting of several subregions (Heilbronner et al., 2016; Izquierdo, 2017; Murphy and Deutch, 2018; Rudebeck and Murray, 2011a; Walton et al., 2011), and medial OFC is implicated in signaling common currency value by human imaging studies (Levy and Glimcher, 2011; Plassmann et al., 2010; Plassmann et al., 2007) and in mediating value-guided behaviors in rats (Bradfield et al., 2015; Münster and Hauber, 2017), monkeys (Noonan et al., 2010) and humans (Camille et al., 2011; Noonan et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to literature on OFC anatomy and function.

claim: Medial OFC is implicated in signaling common currency value by human imaging studies.
source: The OFC is increasingly recognized as consisting of several subregions (Heilbronner et al., 2016; Izquierdo, 2017; Murphy and Deutch, 2018; Rudebeck and Murray, 2011a; Walton et al., 2011), and medial OFC is implicated in signaling common currency value by human imaging studies (Levy and Glimcher, 2011; Plassmann et al., 2010; Plassmann et al., 2007) and in mediating value-guided behaviors in rats (Bradfield et al., 2015; Münster and Hauber, 2017), monkeys (Noonan et al., 2010) and humans (Camille et al., 2011; Noonan et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to human imaging studies.

claim: Medial OFC mediates value-guided behaviors in rats, monkeys, and humans.
source: The OFC is increasingly recognized as consisting of several subregions (Heilbronner et al., 2016; Izquierdo, 2017; Murphy and Deutch, 2018; Rudebeck and Murray, 2011a; Walton et al., 2011), and medial OFC is implicated in signaling common currency value by human imaging studies (Levy and Glimcher, 2011; Plassmann et al., 2010; Plassmann et al., 2007) and in mediating value-guided behaviors in rats (Bradfield et al., 2015; Münster and Hauber, 2017), monkeys (Noonan et al., 2010) and humans (Camille et al., 2011; Noonan et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to studies in multiple species.

claim: Medial OFC is important for using information about outcomes to guide behavior when those outcomes are hidden.
source: Indeed, the comparable part of OFC in rats, located along the base of the medial wall (Heilbronner et al., 2016; Stalnaker et al., 2015), has recently been shown to be important for using information about outcomes to guide behavior when those outcomes are hidden (Bradfield et al., 2015), risky (Stopper and Floresco, 2014), or temporally delayed, although there are conflicting results for this latter finding (Mar et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to studies on medial OFC function in rats.

claim: Six male Long-Evans rats were used in the experiment.
source: Six male Long-Evans rats (275 – 300 g, Charles River Laboratories), aged approximately 3 months at the start of the experiment, were trained and tested at the National Institute on Drug Abuse Intramural Research Program (Baltimore, MD) in accordance with the National Institute of Health guidelines determined by the Animal Care and Use Committee.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the experimental subjects.

claim: Rats were trained on an economic choice task that mimics procedures used in monkeys.
source: To test whether medial OFC is critical for economic choice behavior we inactivated it while rats performed an economic choice task, developed previously (Gardner et al., 2017) to mimic procedures used in monkeys (Padoa-Schioppa and Assad, 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to the task development and the original monkey studies.

claim: In the economic choice task, rats learned to choose between different numbers of flavored food pellets.
source: In this task, rats learned to choose between different numbers of flavored food pellets, providing the opportunity to precisely measure each rats' relative preferences between different goods.
evidence: This is a direct description of the task design.

claim: Each offer in the task consisted of two symbols that conveyed pellet flavors and numbers.
source: On each trial within the task, an offer was displayed on a pair of 3.5' touchscreens situated on either side of a central nosepoke. Each offer consisted of two symbols that conveyed two pieces of information: 1) the pellet flavors in the offer (banana, bacon, grain, chocolate, grape or cellulose), indicated by the shape of each symbol, and 2) the number of pellets of each flavor in the offer (1,2,3,4,6 and sometimes 8), indicated by the segmentations of each symbol (Figure 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by the text description and reference to Figure 1A showing the task design.

claim: Rats were required to nosepoke for 1s while the offer was displayed before making a choice.
source: Rats were required to nosepoke for 1s while the offer was displayed, after which they were able to make a choice by touching the screen with the preferred option.
evidence: This is a direct description of the task procedure.

claim: Each session consisted of 11 offers in which two food pellet flavors were presented in different ratios.
source: Each session consisted of 11 offers in which two food pellet flavors were presented in different ratios.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the experimental design.

claim: Rats learned six visual cue-pellet pairings.
source: Rats learned six visual cue –pellet pairings, and experienced the 15 possible pairings of the six pellet-types across training and testing.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the training procedure.

claim: Rats displayed rational economic choice behavior within the task.
source: We have previously demonstrated that within this task rats display rational economic choice behavior (Gardner et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to the authors' prior published work.

claim: Within individual sessions, rats showed a clear change in preference for the two pellet-types across the range of offers given.
source: Within individual sessions, rats showed a clear change in preference for the two pellet-types across the range of offers given.
evidence: This is a direct statement about observed behavior.

claim: The indifference point was used as an estimate of the relative valuation of the two pellet flavors.
source: The offer for which rats showed no preference for the two offer-types, referred to as the indifference point (IP), was used as an estimate of the relative valuation of the two pellet flavors.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the analytical approach.

claim: Indifference points between particular pairs of food pellets for individual rats ranged widely from 1:1 to greater than 8:1.
source: Notably, indifference points between particular pairs of food pellets for individual rats ranged widely from 1:1 to greater than 8:1, suggesting that the rats were choosing based on internal subjective values (only IPs <= 6 were included in analyses).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the observed data range.

claim: The wide range of indifference points suggests that rats were choosing based on internal subjective values.
source: Notably, indifference points between particular pairs of food pellets for individual rats ranged widely from 1:1 to greater than 8:1, suggesting that the rats were choosing based on internal subjective values (only IPs <= 6 were included in analyses).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observed data range.

claim: Indifference points were stable across sessions.
source: Further these indifference points were stable across sessions and exhibited transitivity across offer pairs with shared constituents, a property often taken as an indicator of rational decision making.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the observed stability of the data.

claim: Indifference points exhibited transitivity across offer pairs with shared constituents.
source: Further these indifference points were stable across sessions and exhibited transitivity across offer pairs with shared constituents, a property often taken as an indicator of rational decision making.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the observed property of the data.

claim: Transitivity is a property often taken as an indicator of rational decision making.
source: Further these indifference points were stable across sessions and exhibited transitivity across offer pairs with shared constituents, a property often taken as an indicator of rational decision making.
evidence: This is a statement about established knowledge in the field.

claim: AAV-CaMKIIa-eNpHR3.0-eYFP was infused into medial OFC bilaterally.
source: AAV-CaMKIIa-eNpHR3.0-eYFP was then infused into medial OFC bilaterally, and fiberoptic probes were implanted just above each injection site (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the surgical procedure, with reference to Figure 1C.

claim: Fiberoptic probes were implanted just above each injection site.
source: AAV-CaMKIIa-eNpHR3.0-eYFP was then infused into medial OFC bilaterally, and fiberoptic probes were implanted just above each injection site (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the surgical procedure, with reference to Figure 1C.

claim: Rats were retrained to pre-surgical performance levels after a 2-3 week postoperative recovery period.
source: Following surgery and a 2 – 3 week postoperative recovery period, rats were retrained to pre-surgical performance levels (~5 weeks, see Materials and methods), then we began sessions in which we tested the effects of inactivating medial OFC.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the experimental timeline.

claim: The testing phase of the experiment lasted approximately 8 weeks.
source: This phase of the experiment, lasting ~8 weeks, was designed as follows: rats experienced three separate pellet-pairs for three consecutive days for a total of 9 test sessions (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the experimental duration, with reference to Figure 1B.

claim: Rats experienced each pellet pair in an initial warm up session followed by two test sessions with either a dummy cable or a patent light-transmitting cable.
source: Rats experienced each pair in an initial warm up session that was followed by two test sessions in which they were connected to either a dummy cable, which was blocked at the ferrule to prevent light delivery to the brain, or a patent light-transmitting cable, which was unblocked at the ferrule allowing light to enter the brain.
evidence: This is a direct description of the experimental design.

claim: Cable type was counterbalanced across days.
source: Cable type was counterbalanced across days.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the experimental design.

claim: Each session was separated into trials in which the laser was either on or off.
source: Each session was also separated into trials in which the laser was either on or off.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the experimental design.

claim: During laser-on trials, green light (16-18 mW, 532 nm) was delivered to the fiberoptic cables.
source: During laser-on trials, green light (16 – 18 mW, 532 nm) was delivered to the fiberoptic cables.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the experimental procedure.

claim: Laser onset co-occurred with the onset of the white noise that signaled that a trial could be initiated.
source: Laser onset co-occurred with the onset of the white noise that signaled that a trial could be initiated.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the experimental timing.

claim: The laser was terminated when the rat contacted one of the touch screens, with a 300 ms linear ramp down to minimize rebound excitation.
source: The laser was terminated when the rat contacted one of the touch screens, and termination included a period of 300 ms during which the power was reduced linearly, a protocol which has been shown to minimize or prevent rebound excitation (Chuong et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the experimental procedure, with citation to support the protocol.

claim: There was very little difference in choice behavior between laser-on and laser-off trials in example sessions.
source: An initial examination of data from example sessions (Figure 2A, blocked and patent cable sessions from consecutive days on the same pellet pair) revealed very little difference in choice behavior between the laser-on and –off trials, and the averaged choice behavior (Figure 2B) supported this assessment.
evidence: This claim is supported by reference to Figure 2A and 2B showing the behavioral data.

claim: A two-factor repeated measures ANOVA on indifference points revealed no significant main effects of Laser or Fiber, nor any significant interaction.
source: To determine whether this occurred with medial OFC inhibition, we ran a two-factor repeated measures ANOVA on 50 pairs of sessions with factors Laser (laser-on/-off) and Fiber (blocked/patent). This analysis revealed no significant main effects of either Laser (F(1,147) = 1.31, p=0.25) or Fiber (F(1,147) = 1.03, p=0.31) nor any significant effect of the critical interaction term Laser*Fiber (F(1,147) = 0.75, p=0.39).
evidence: This claim is supported by the statistical analysis results presented in the text.

claim: There were no significant differences in indifference points when comparing the current groups to eYFP controls from a prior experiment.
source: In addition, at the reviewers' request, we also compared the current groups to eYFP controls, identically trained and tested in a prior experiment, and there were no significant differences (Figure 3—figure supplement 1, see Supplementary file 1 for ANOVA results)(Gardner et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by reference to Figure 3—figure supplement 1 and Supplementary file 1, with citation to prior work.

claim: None of the four post-hoc simple effects comparisons reached significance for indifference points.
source: We also ran post-hoc simple effects comparing levels across each factor of the design. None of the four comparisons reached significance (paired t-test, n = 50, p>0.14, β <1e-10 for a shift to 1:1); this included the primary comparison of interest, laser-on vs laser-off trials in the patent cable condition (p=0.90).
evidence: This claim is supported by the statistical analysis results presented in the text.

claim: The indifference point increased by only 0.3% during the laser-on trials in the patent fiber condition.
source: The indifference point increased by only 0.3% during the laser-on trials (mean IP for the patent fiber and laser-off trials: 1.649, mean IP for laser-on trials: 1.65), an effect which is well within the confidence interval (CI: [1.56 1.74], which corresponds ±10.6% shift of the IP).
evidence: This claim is supported by the quantitative data analysis presented in the text.

claim: The test would have found about a one-tenth change in the average preference significant.
source: Importantly, our test would have found about a one-tenth change in the average preference significant.
evidence: This is a statement about the statistical power of the test.

claim: When sessions with IPs close to 1:1 were excluded, the ANOVA still found no significant effects on indifference points.
source: To test this possibility, we removed sessions within a conservative 1.45:1 preference based on an empirical distribution of variance (see Materials and Methods, 19 session pairs were excluded) and reran the two-way ANOVA. Despite our focus on sessions with strong preferences (mean IP for all conditions: 2.07), this analysis still found neither significant main effects (Fiber: F(1,90) = 1.57, p=0.21; Laser: F(1,90) = 1.19, p=0.28) nor any interaction (F(1,90) = 0.87, p=0.35).
evidence: This claim is supported by the statistical analysis results presented in the text.

claim: A three-way ANOVA with factors Laser, Fiber and Time revealed no significant effect of the three-way interaction or any two-way interactions on indifference points.
source: A three-way ANOVA with factors Laser, Fiber and Time revealed no significant effect of the critical three-way interaction of Laser*Fiber*Time (F(2,141) = 0.08, p=0.92), nor any of the two-way interactions (Laser*Time: F(2,141) = 1.58, p=0.21; Fiber*Time F(2,141) = 0.35, p=0.70; Laser*Fiber (F1,141)=0.73, p=0.40).
evidence: This claim is supported by the statistical analysis results presented in the text.

claim: There was a main effect of Time on indifference points, likely due to variations in preferences across the three pellets used for each time block.
source: There was a main effect of Time (F(1,141) = 5.97, p=5.0e-3), which is likely due to the variations in the preferences across the three pellets used for each of the three time blocks.
evidence: This claim is supported by the statistical analysis results and the authors' interpretation.

claim: When analyzing only the first 29.9% of each session, the two-way ANOVA found no significant effect of inactivation on indifference points.
source: To determine whether an effect of inactivation was apparent at the beginning of a behavioral session, we included the minimum number of trials for each offer for which we could determine a reasonable estimate of the IP (n = 4 for each of the 11 offers, for both laser-on and –off trial-types, 88 trials total) which was on average, the first 29.9% of the session. We then reran the two-way ANOVA test on this early session behavior. Neither the critical interaction effect of Laser*Fiber nor the main effects displayed a significant effect of inactivation (see Supplementary file 2 for ANOVA results).
evidence: This claim is supported by reference to Supplementary file 2 containing the statistical results.

claim: A repeated measures two-way ANOVA on inverse slope measures revealed no significant main effects or interaction.
source: A repeated measures two-way ANOVA on these measures revealed no significant main effect of either Laser (F(1,147) = 0.69, p=0.41) or Fiber (F(1,147) = 0.11, p=0.74) nor any significant effect of the critical interaction term Laser*Fiber (F(1,147) = 0.26, p=0.61).
evidence: This claim is supported by the statistical analysis results presented in the text.

claim: There were no significant differences in inverse slope when comparing the current groups to eYFP controls from a prior experiment.
source: In addition, at the reviewers' request, we also compared the current groups to eYFP controls, identically trained and tested in a prior experiment, and there were no significant differences (Figure 4—figure supplement 1, see Supplementary file 1 for ANOVA results)(Gardner et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by reference to Figure 4—figure supplement 1 and Supplementary file 1, with citation to prior work.

claim: Simple effects analysis showed no significant differences in inverse slope across conditions.
source: Simple effects within and across factors also showed no significant differences (4 paired t-tests, n = 50, p>=0.29).
evidence: This claim is supported by the statistical analysis results presented in the text.

claim: When sessions with IPs close to 1:1 were excluded, the ANOVA still found no significant effects on inverse slope.
source: We again tested whether the slope might be more affected by inactivation during sessions in which the IP is reasonably distant from equal or 1:1 preference (Figure 4D). We used the same empirical threshold, 1.45:1, that we used for testing the IPs resulting in 19 fewer session pairs entering into the analysis. We repeated the ANOVA and again found no significant effects (Laser: F(1,90) = 0.19, p=0.66; Fiber: F(1,90) = 0.74, p=0.39; Laser*Fiber: F(1,90) < 0.01 , p=0.98), and testing of the simple effects across conditions showed no effects as well (4 paired t-tests, n = 31, p>0.55).
evidence: This claim is supported by the statistical analysis results and reference to Figure 4D.

claim: A three-way ANOVA with factors Laser, Fiber and Time revealed no significant effect of the three-way interaction or any two-way interactions on inverse slope.
source: A three-way ANOVA with factors Laser, Fiber and Time revealed no significant effect of the critical three-way interaction of Laser*Fiber*Time (F(2,141) = 0.06, p=0.94), nor any of the two-way interactions (Laser*Time: F(2,141) = 0.04, p=0.96; Fiber*Time F(2,141) = 2.11, p=0.12; Laser*Fiber (F1,141)=0.27, p=0.61).
evidence: This claim is supported by the statistical analysis results presented in the text.

claim: There was no main effect of Time on inverse slope.
source: Unlike the IP, there was no main effect of Time (F(1,141) = 0.44, p=0.64), further indicating this effect was due to variations in the preferences of the pellets used across the time blocks.
evidence: This claim is supported by the statistical analysis results presented in the text.

claim: When analyzing only the first 29.9% of each session, the critical interaction effect of Laser*Fiber on inverse slope was not significant.
source: Finally, we looked at whether the slope was affected by inactivation just at the beginning of the session. As explained for the IP analysis, we narrowed our data to the first 4 trials of each offer (on average the first 29.9% of each session) and reran the two-way ANOVA test on this early session behavior. The critical interaction effect of Laser*Fiber was not significant.
evidence: This claim is supported by reference to Supplementary file 2 containing the statistical results.

claim: The main effect of Laser on inverse slope was significant in the early session analysis.
source: The main effect of Laser was significant. Further analysis revealed a significant difference in the simple effects between the laser-on and –off trials in the blocked fiber condition, but not in the patent fiber condition (see Supplementary file 2 for ANOVA results).
evidence: This claim is supported by reference to Supplementary file 2 containing the statistical results.

claim: Rats show transitive behavior on the economic choice task when choosing between multiple pellet-types across days.
source: Rats show transitive behavior on our task when choosing between multiple pellet-types across days.
evidence: This is a direct statement about observed behavior.

claim: Transitive behavior implies that rats have a consistent and relatively stable value space onto which they map different goods.
source: This implies that rats have a consistent and relatively stable value space onto which they map different goods in our task.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observed transitive behavior.

claim: The rats' behavior was generally transitive, with only small, seemingly random fluctuations between laser-on and laser-off trials.
source: A comparison of these points for laser-on versus laser-off trials in blocked versus patent sessions demonstrates that the rats' behavior was again generally transitive, with only small, seemingly random fluctuations between the laser-on and laser-off trial types.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the observed transitivity data.

claim: The small fluctuations in transitivity were unaffected by whether or not the fiber was patent to allow inactivation.
source: Critically the points and these small fluctuations were unaffected by whether or not the fiber was patent to allow inactivation.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the observed transitivity data.

claim: A repeated-measures, two-way ANOVA on transitivity values found no main effects or interaction.
source: To confirm this, we performed a repeated-measures, two-way ANOVA comparing the single transitivity values; this analysis found neither main effects nor any interaction (Laser: F(1,42) = 0.54, p=0.47; Fiber: F(1,42) = 3.21, p=0.08; Laser*Fiber: F(1,42) = 0.54, p=0.47).
evidence: This claim is supported by the statistical analysis results presented in the text.

claim: A repeated measures ANOVA on the distances between paired transitivity points found no effect of fiber type.
source: To determine whether these distances were affected by inactivation, we ran a repeated measures ANOVA with the fiber-type as the single factor on the distances of the pairs of laser-on and –off trials and found no effect of Fiber: F(1,14) = 0.13, p=0.73.
evidence: This claim is supported by the statistical analysis results presented in the text.

claim: Resting membrane potential was significantly hyperpolarized by 10 s light exposure in medial OFC neurons expressing NpHR-YFP.
source: We then performed whole cell current clamp recordings in neurons (n = 10) transfected with NpHR-YFP and assessed the effect of 593 nm light exposure (Figure 6A). Resting membrane potential was significantly hyperpolarized by 10 s light exposure (One-way ANOVA, F(1.06,9.49) = 26.42, p= 5.0e-4).
evidence: This claim is supported by the electrophysiology data and statistical analysis, with reference to Figure 6A.

claim: The hyperpolarization effect was maximal at the onset but maintained significant hyperpolarization in the steady state condition.
source: The effect was maximal at the onset (peak) but maintained significant hyperpolarization in the steady state condition.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the observed electrophysiology data.

claim: Repetitive firing activity elicited by current injection was significantly inhibited by concurrent light exposure.
source: In addition, repetitive firing activity elicited by a square pulse current injection of 400 pA was significantly inhibited by concurrent light exposure (Paired t-test, t(5) = 4.05, p=0.01).
evidence: This claim is supported by the electrophysiology data and statistical analysis.

claim: Following light exposure, direct current injection elicited fewer spikes per unit of current as evidenced by a rightward shift in the input-output curve.
source: Following light exposure, direct current injection elicited fewer spikes per unit of current as evidenced by a rightward shift in the input-output curve (Figure 6B)(Two-way repeated measures ANOVA, F(11, 55)=4.3, p=1.0e-4).
evidence: This claim is supported by the electrophysiology data and statistical analysis, with reference to Figure 6B.

claim: A repeated measures ANOVA on the progressive ratio breaking point revealed a significant main effect of Fiber.
source: A repeated measures ANOVA (rat and run were used as blocking factors) performed on the breaking point, corresponding to the number of pellets achieved, revealed a significant main effect of Fiber (F(1,10) = 9.97, p=0.01).
evidence: This claim is supported by the statistical analysis results presented in the text.

claim: The effect of fiber type on progressive ratio breaking point was robust with 7 of 8 blocked/patent pairs trending in the same direction.
source: This effect was robust with 7 of the eight blocked/patent pairs trending in the same direction (Figure 7A left).
evidence: This claim is supported by reference to Figure 7A showing the individual data points.

claim: An ANOVA on total lever presses in the progressive ratio task revealed a significant main effect of Fiber.
source: An ANOVA with the same design yet performed on the total lever presses also revealed a significant main effect of Fiber (F(1,10) = 7.85, p=0.02) (Figure 7B right).
evidence: This claim is supported by the statistical analysis results and reference to Figure 7B.

claim: Prolonged inhibition did not result in decreased motor activity as measured by inter-press intervals.
source: Importantly prolonged inhibition did not result in decreased motor activity; Figure (7B top) shows histograms of the inter-press intervals (IPIs) for the two conditions in which there appears to be no discernable difference. A two sample Kolmogorov-Smirnov test on the cumulative distributions of the IPIs (Figure 7B bottom) revealed no significant effect (D(1436,1045) = 0.028, p=0.74).
evidence: This claim is supported by the statistical analysis results and reference to Figure 7B.

claim: A repeated measures ANOVA showed no effect of inactivation on food consumption.
source: To do this, animals were given a bowl of 20 grams of food pellets in the conditioning box for 30 min to assess pellet consumption with and without inhibition. This test was repeated 4 times with blocked and patent cables (counterbalanced). A repeated measures ANOVA (with rat and run as blocking factors) showed no effect of inactivation on food consumption (F(1,10) = 0.20, p=0.66).
evidence: This claim is supported by the statistical analysis results presented in the text.

claim: Transient optogenetic inactivation of medial OFC on randomly selected trials had no effect on economic choice behavior.
source: In the current study, we employed a rodent version of the economic choice task used to demonstrate neural correlates of economic value in primates (Padoa-Schioppa and Assad, 2006) to test whether medial OFC makes a critical contribution to economic choice behavior. We found that transient optogenetic inactivation of medial OFC on randomly selected trials had no effect.
evidence: This is the primary finding of the study, supported by all the statistical analyses presented.

claim: Inactivation in the same rats altered performance on a progressive ratio task known to be sensitive to medial OFC manipulations.
source: Inactivation in the same rats altered performance on a progressive ratio task known to be sensitive to medial OFC manipulations, and post-mortem testing confirmed that medial OFC neurons in these rats exhibited viral expression and light-sensitive reduction in spiking activity.
evidence: This claim is supported by the progressive ratio data and the electrophysiology data.

claim: Post-mortem testing confirmed that medial OFC neurons in these rats exhibited viral expression and light-sensitive reduction in spiking activity.
source: Inactivation in the same rats altered performance on a progressive ratio task known to be sensitive to medial OFC manipulations, and post-mortem testing confirmed that medial OFC neurons in these rats exhibited viral expression and light-sensitive reduction in spiking activity.
evidence: This claim is supported by the histology and electrophysiology data.

claim: Medial OFC is not necessary for economic choice in well-trained rats.
source: Together these data show that the medial OFC is not necessary for economic choice in well-trained rats.
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study, based on the combined results.

claim: The current study builds on a prior report that optogenetic inactivation of lateral OFC also had no discernable effect on economic choice.
source: The current study builds on our prior report that optogenetic inactivation of lateral OFC also had no discernable effect on economic choice in this setting (Gardner et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to the authors' prior published work.

claim: Inactivation of lateral OFC was motivated by reports that neural activity in lateral OFC correlates with value during economic choice.
source: Inactivation of lateral OFC was motivated by influential reports that neural activity in lateral OFC correlates with value during economic choice (McGinty et al., 2016; Padoa-Schioppa, 2009; Padoa-Schioppa and Assad, 2006; Padoa-Schioppa and Assad, 2008; Rich and Wallis, 2016; Tremblay and Schultz, 1999; Xie and Padoa-Schioppa, 2016), and the associated proposal that lateral OFC was central to normal decision-making in this context (Padoa-Schioppa, 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to the literature.

claim: Economic value is proposed to be equivalent to the value revealed by devaluation underlying model-based behavior.
source: Implicit in this proposal is that economic value is equivalent to the value revealed by devaluation underlying so-called model-based behavior.
evidence: This is an implicit assumption identified by the authors in the neuroeconomics framework.

claim: Model-based behavior typically depends on lateral OFC in both rats and primates.
source: Such behavior typically depends on this part of OFC in both rats and primates (Gallagher et al., 1999; Izquierdo et al., 2004; Machado and Bachevalier, 2007; Pickens et al., 2005; Pickens et al., 2003; Rudebeck et al., 2013; West et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to studies in rats and primates.

claim: Lateral OFC inactivation abolished changes in behavior due to devaluation without any effect on economic choice behavior.
source: Yet we found that we could inactivate lateral OFC and abolish changes in behavior due to devaluation without any effect on economic choice behavior.
evidence: This claim is based on the authors' prior experimental results.

claim: The result that lateral OFC inactivation did not affect economic choice did not support lateral OFC as a critical, single bottleneck for calculating economic value.
source: While this result did not support the lateral OFC as a critical, single bottleneck in which economic value is calculated, it left open whether other parts of the OFC might be performing this function.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the prior experimental results.

claim: The OFC is now recognized to be a large area, potentially divisible into discrete subregions mediating discrete functions.
source: The OFC is now recognized to be a large area, potentially divisible into discrete subregions mediating discrete functions (Heilbronner et al., 2016; Izquierdo, 2017; Murphy and Deutch, 2018; Rudebeck and Murray, 2011b; Walton et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to the literature on OFC organization.

claim: Within the OFC framework, medial OFC is increasingly associated with representing value.
source: Within this framework, the medial OFC is increasingly associated with representing value.
evidence: This is a statement about the current understanding in the field.

claim: Lesions to medial OFC in monkeys disrupt value-guided decisions whereas lateral OFC lesions cause deficits in other more subtle functions.
source: Further, lesions to medial OFC in monkeys disrupt value-guided decisions whereas lateral OFC lesions on the same behavior cause deficits in other more subtle functions, such as credit-assignment (Noonan et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a study in monkeys.

claim: Medial OFC is necessary for appropriate valuation during acquisition of cue-outcome pairings.
source: Other studies have shown that medial OFC is necessary for appropriate valuation during acquisition of cue-outcome pairings (Baylis and Gaffan, 1991), and also following selective satiation of one outcome during a choice task (Rudebeck and Murray, 2011a).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to studies on medial OFC function.

claim: Damage to medial OFC in humans is associated with deficits in valuation and changes in economic decision-making.
source: Damage to medial OFC in humans is associated with similar deficits, as well as changes in economic decision-making (Camille et al., 2011; Fellows and Farah, 2007; Noonan et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to human lesion studies.

claim: Despite promising background data, inactivating medial OFC had no effect on economic choice.
source: Yet despite the promising background data, we again failed to find any effect of inactivating the OFC on economic choice.
evidence: This is a summary statement of the main finding.

claim: Rats exhibited similar preferences among groups of flavored food pellets with or without medial OFC online.
source: Rats exhibited similar preferences among groups of flavored food pellets with or without medial OFC online, at least as indexed by indifference points, the steepness of the curves relating the two pellets, and the transitivity of the choices.
evidence: This is a summary of the behavioral results across multiple measures.

claim: There was a reduction in the progressive ratio breakpoint with medial OFC inactivation.
source: This was true despite a reduction in the progressive ratio breakpoint in the same rats with inactivation, an effect that would traditionally be interpreted as an effect on valuation.
evidence: This claim is supported by the progressive ratio data.

claim: The results show that medial OFC is not the critical bottleneck for calculating a single common currency value to guide economic choice.
source: These results show that medial OFC is also not the critical bottleneck for calculating a single common currency value to guide economic choice.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the combined results.

claim: The data point strongly to the possibility that economic value and resultant decision-making depend on parallel processing in multiple regions.
source: Instead, these and the prior data point strongly to the possibility that economic value and the resultant decision-making depend on parallel processing in multiple regions (Hunt and Hayden, 2017).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the results, supported by citation to a relevant theoretical paper.

claim: Parallel processing would be predicted if the value judgement underlying economic choice reflected a variety of associative information.
source: Such parallel processing would be predicted if the value judgement underlying economic choice, at least as assayed in this task, reflected a variety of associative information (e.g. Pavlovian and instrumental, model-based and model-free, habitual and goal-directed).
evidence: This is a theoretical prediction based on the results.

claim: The economic choice task used here does not try to limit or control the associative information at play.
source: This is likely because the economic choice task used here, and those employed in other settings, generally do not try to limit or control the associative information at play.
evidence: This is an observation about the task design.

claim: Different types of associative information do not generally converge into a single common brain region but are mediated by somewhat non-overlapping brain circuits.
source: Tasks that employ such controls have clearly demonstrated that these different types of associative information do not generally converge into a single common brain region, but instead are mediated by somewhat non-overlapping brain circuits, each capable of mediating behavior somewhat independently, particularly in simple or poorly-controlled settings.
evidence: This is a statement about established knowledge in the field.

claim: The results are more consistent with a distributed representation of value.
source: Our results are more consistent with this sort of distributed representation of value.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the results in the context of existing theories.

claim: The processing in lateral and medial OFC may still be important for economic choice behavior, but a better controlled task is necessary to reveal the critical contributions.
source: Of course, this does not mean that the processing demonstrated in this and similar tasks in lateral and medial OFC is not important for economic choice behavior. Rather it simply means that a better controlled form of the task is necessary in order to reveal the critical contributions these areas (and others) each make to the very general function of economic choice.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation about future research directions.

claim: It has been suggested that orbital areas are critical when choices are novel, rapidly changing, or involve elements that have never been experienced.
source: For example, it has been suggested that orbital areas are critical when choices are novel, rapidly changing, or involve elements that have never been experienced – such as the evocative tea-jelly and snail-porridge prepared by Behrens and colleagues (Baylis and Gaffan, 1991; Rudebeck and Murray, 2011b; Fellows and Farah, 2007; Noonan et al., 2010); Chau et al., 2014; Barron et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to studies suggesting this role for orbital areas.

claim: The dissociation between economic choice and OFC-dependent behaviors occurs because these behaviors require a form of inference or estimation not necessary in a well-trained subject in the standard economic choice task.
source: Viewed in this light, the dissociation here (and also in our prior study) between economic choice and OFC-dependent behaviors, such as progressive ratio and Pavlovian devaluation for lOFC, occurs because these behaviors require a form of inference or estimation that is not necessary in a well-trained subject in the standard economic choice task like that used here.
evidence: This is a theoretical interpretation of the dissociation observed in the results.

claim: Economic choices will depend on a particular region to the extent the choice emphasizes the processing dependent on that area.
source: Economic choices will depend on a particular region to the extent the choice emphasizes the processing dependent on that area.
evidence: This is a theoretical statement about how brain regions contribute to economic choice.

claim: The role of different subregions within OFC in economic choice behavior would be identical to their roles in other value-based behaviors.
source: In this regard, the role of different subregions within OFC in economic choice behavior would be identical to their roles in other value-based behaviors.
evidence: This is a theoretical statement about OFC function.
